claims.text: The initial material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy-alloy thin film made by sputtering.
Films produced by conventional sputtering have relatively low or minimal nanoporosity.
Adjusting deposition rate and substrate temperature can intentionally induce significant nanoporosity in FeMnNiGeSi-type films.
Controlled processing conditions can alter phase stability or transition behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Increasing nanoporosity increases the film's surface-to-volume ratio and interfacial area.
The increased surface and interfacial area improves heat-exchange rates.
Enhanced surface architecture reduces thermal gradients during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Enhanced surface architecture reduces local stresses in the film.
Reduced thermal gradients and local stresses produce a smoother magnetostructural transition.
A smoother magnetostructural transition mitigates the abrupt entropy change and reduces hysteresis.
Nanoporous samples will have a broader and less sharply peaked magnetocaloric response than baseline films.
Nanoporous samples will have lower hysteresis losses than baseline films.
Nanoporous samples will equilibrate thermally faster than baseline films.
Heat transfer and hysteresis losses are relevant performance considerations for magnetic-refrigeration materials.
The predicted effects should occur under low applied fields near the magnetostructural transition in films 100 nm to 1 µm thick.
The effects may differ in bulk samples because bulk samples have a lower surface-to-volume ratio.
The magnitude of entropy and hysteresis changes depends on the extent and uniformity of the introduced nanoporosity.
TEM or AFM can be used to compare porosity between intervention and control films.
Magnetometry, calorimetry, and thermal-response testing can compare hysteresis, entropy-change magnitude and width, and heat-exchange rates.

Failure of the nanoporous samples to show statistically significant hysteresis reduction, improved heat exchange, or appreciable transition smoothing or broadening relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
